title: Three perfect days in San Francisco
dek: Mozart at the opera, tea at the Ferry Building and a cliff walk at Lands End: a mid-November weekend that keeps to the west side and the bay, well away from last week's North Beach.

hero.caption: The Japanese Tea Garden in Golden Gate Park, Saturday afternoon's stop before the early November closing.

intro:
Mid-November is when San Francisco gets quieter in a good way. The summer fog has moved on, the first rains of the season usually arrive, and the city turns to indoor pleasures without giving up its coast. This weekend has a good share of both.

San Francisco Opera's revival of *The Marriage of Figaro* plays Friday night and Sunday afternoon at the War Memorial Opera House, conducted by Sebastian Weigle in his company debut. On Saturday and Sunday the SF International Tea Festival fills the Ferry Building with more than 30 tea makers, and the Renegade Craft Fair sets up its winter edition at Fort Mason, an early start on holiday shopping. Friday evening, Yerba Buena Gardens hosts a free Bhangra & Beats Diwali Night Market.

The plan below keeps each day in one part of town. Friday stays in Japantown and Pacific Heights before the opera. Saturday heads west, to the cliffs at Lands End, the Chinese bakeries and bookshops of Clement Street, and the Japanese Tea Garden. Sunday follows the bay from the Ferry Building to the Exploratorium, then rides the T Third line to Dogpatch for the last day of a type-design show at Letterform Archive. The Warriors are on the road all weekend, so Mission Bay and the Muni trains around Chase Center will be calmer than usual. Bring a rain shell and a warm layer, and book the opera and Friday dinner now.

days.title: Friday: Japantown, Pacific Heights and Figaro
days.intro: A slow morning on the hill above Fillmore Street, ramen and bookshops in the Japan Center, and an early dinner before a long night of Mozart.

stops.name: Jina Bakes
stops.text: A small Japanese and Korean bakery on Webster Street. The Infatuation says its kalbijjim croissant, stuffed with braised short rib from nearby Daeho, topped with mozzarella and torched, "will change your life, full stop." If that is too much for breakfast, have the hojicha or matcha cream puff, or the injeolmi croissant coated in roasted soybean powder, and take a bag of butter mochi for later. Check the day's hours before you walk over.

stops.name: Pacific Heights: Alta Plaza and Lafayette Park
stops.text: Walk north up Fillmore Street, which climbs steeply past cafés and boutiques, to Alta Plaza Park. Its terraced top looks out over the city's rooftops toward the bay. Then head east along Washington Street, past some of the grandest houses in town, to Lafayette Park, another hilltop lawn with long views. It is a free, unhurried hour and a half of steep streets and good views. Wear shoes with grip if the pavement is wet.

stops.name: Marufuku Ramen
stops.text: The original Marufuku opened in the Japan Center in 2017, and The Infatuation still calls its creamy Hakata-style tonkotsu an "intensely porky flavor bomb." Order the classic bowl with an egg and let the thin noodles soak up the broth. There is almost always a line, so join the waitlist as soon as you arrive. If it is very long, Hinodeya, in the same mall, serves a lighter dashi broth and takes walk-ins only.

stops.name: Japan Center and Kinokuniya
stops.text: The Japan Center malls opened in 1968, and Kinokuniya has anchored them since 1969. It is the chain's oldest US store, with about 11,000 square feet of Japanese and English books, manga, art books, magazines and good stationery. Then walk through the rest of the malls for knives, ceramics, snacks and capsule-toy machines, and step out to the Peace Plaza to see the five-tiered Peace Pagoda. Leave time for a rest before dinner.

stops.name: State Bird Provisions
stops.text: Stuart Brioza and Nicole Krasinski's restaurant, which holds a Michelin star in the 2026 guide, serves seasonal California cooking dim-sum style: small plates come round on carts and trays, and you point at what you want. Take the dumplings and a savory pancake as they pass, then order the famous fried quail from the menu. The first seating at 5:30 leaves plenty of time to get to the opera. Book well ahead, especially for a Friday.

stops.name: The Marriage of Figaro at the War Memorial Opera House
stops.text: Michael Cavanagh's production returns with Peter Kellner as Figaro, Slávka Zámečníková as Susanna and Olivia Smith as the Countess, conducted by Sebastian Weigle. Mozart's comedy of one long, crowded wedding day is sung in Italian with English supertitles. The 1932 house is a ten-minute ride from Fillmore Street on the 22 or 38 bus. Allow for the running time of 3 hours 45 minutes, with two intermissions, and plan a taxi or late Muni home.

days.title: Saturday: the Richmond, from cliff to tea garden
days.intro: The city's western end: croissants, a coastal walk above the Golden Gate, Clement Street and the park, with the 38 Geary bus tying it together.

stops.name: Arsicault Bakery
stops.text: Armando Lacayo's corner bakery on Arguello Boulevard made its name with croissants, and The Infatuation's Richmond guide, updated in October, still sends people here for the almond croissant and the kouign amann. Expect a line on a Saturday morning; it moves, and arriving early helps before the best pastries sell out. Eat on the bench outside, then catch the 38 Geary bus west toward the ocean.

stops.name: Lands End Trail and the Sutro Baths ruins
stops.text: From the Lands End Lookout on Point Lobos Avenue, walk down to the concrete ruins of the Sutro Baths, Adolph Sutro's giant glass-roofed bathhouse, which burned in 1966. Then follow the Coastal Trail east through cypress and along the cliffs, with views across the strait to the Marin Headlands and the Golden Gate Bridge. Two hours covers it at an easy pace. Stairs and side paths can be muddy after rain, and you should stay off the cliff edges.

stops.name: Good Luck Dim Sum
stops.text: A Clement Street dim sum counter that has fed the neighborhood for decades. Get siu mai, barbecue pork buns and the fried sesame balls, and take them to go or eat nearby. It is cheap, fast and very much a neighborhood place, with weekend lines that move quickly. Bring cash, since it takes nothing else.

stops.name: Green Apple Books
stops.text: A Richmond fixture since 1967, with new and used books spread over several rooms and staff picks worth reading. Co-owner Pete Mulvihill put its appeal plainly to the Richmond Review/Sunset Beacon: "Amazon is good at search but terrible to browse." Give it an hour, buy something local for the trip home, then walk south on Eighth Avenue into Golden Gate Park.

stops.name: Japanese Tea Garden
stops.text: The oldest public Japanese garden in the country, dating from the 1894 Midwinter Fair: a steep drum bridge, a five-story pagoda, stone lanterns and maples that may still have some autumn color. Sit in the teahouse with a pot of green tea before the light goes. November hours are 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., with last entry half an hour before closing, so do not dawdle. Weekend admission for non-residents is $16, and San Francisco residents get in free.

stops.name: Lily
stops.text: A Vietnamese restaurant on Clement Street with a modern menu and a full room most nights. Order the pho finished with roasted bone marrow and a salted duck-egg iced coffee, and share a few small plates. It is warm and lively on a Saturday, the right place after an afternoon in the cold park. It takes OpenTable reservations and closes at 9 p.m., so go early.

days.title: Sunday: along the bay to Dogpatch
days.intro: Tea and oysters at the Ferry Building, science on the piers, then the T Third train south for type design and an Italian dinner.

stops.name: SF International Tea Festival at the Ferry Building
stops.text: More than 30 tea makers, among them Imperial Tea Court, Sugimoto Tea Company and K&K Chai, set up in the Ferry Building with hundreds of teas to taste. A ticket buys a porcelain tasting cup and free tastings; funcheap listed Saturday hours of 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., so check Sunday's on the festival site. Arrive at opening, before the crowds, and taste slowly; it is a fine breakfast substitute.

stops.name: Hog Island Oyster Co.
stops.text: The Tomales Bay oyster farm's bar inside the Ferry Building opens at 11 a.m., and an early lunch is the way to get a seat looking out over the bay. Order a dozen raw oysters on the half shell, the clam chowder, and a glass of something dry. Walk-ins only; at 11:45 the wait is usually shortest.

stops.name: Exploratorium
stops.text: A ten-minute walk north along the Embarcadero to Pier 15. The Exploratorium's more than 650 hands-on exhibits are as good for adults as for children: light and sound experiments, a gallery on human behavior, and an outdoor gallery on the forces that shape the city and the bay. It opens at noon on Sundays and closes at 5 p.m. Give it two and a half hours and buy tickets online.

stops.name: Letterform Archive: Type for All!
stops.text: Ride the T Third train south to Dogpatch for the last day of *Type for All! Ten Years of Type West*. The show celebrates the archive's type-design program with fonts from 31 countries, and the archive itself holds one of the best collections of lettering and graphic design anywhere. Sunday gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. and 2 to 6 p.m. Admission is $10. On Sundays, use the call box at 2325 Third Street to be buzzed up to Floor 4R.

stops.name: Piccino
stops.text: The corner restaurant at 22nd and Minnesota has been Dogpatch's neighborhood Italian for years. The Infatuation's August guide recommends the milk-braised pork ragu and the mushroom pizza, and a bottle from the Italian-leaning list goes well with both. Dinner starts at 5 p.m. and the kitchen closes at 8:30 on Sundays, so this is an early, easy end to the weekend. Reserve on Resy.

stay.name: The Ritz-Carlton, San Francisco
stay.text: A 1909 Neoclassical landmark on Nob Hill, with cable cars passing on California Street. Its new lounge, Bruma, opened in October and has live jazz on Friday nights and a Latin band on Saturdays, a good nightcap after the opera. It is quiet and polished, and central to all three days.

stay.name: The Westin St. Francis
stay.text: The grand old hotel on Union Square, open since 1904, with a lobby clock that has been the city's meeting point for generations. It is a straight Muni ride to the opera, the Ferry Building and the T Third line to Dogpatch. Ask for the original building if you like high ceilings, or the tower for views.

stay.name: Hotel Kabuki
stay.text: A Japanese-styled hotel, part of Hyatt's JdV collection, steps from the Japan Center and Friday's whole itinerary. The 38 Geary bus out front runs straight to the Richmond and Lands End on Saturday. It is a calm base for the price, close to the Kabuki cinema and the Fillmore Street shops.

events.name: San Francisco Opera: The Marriage of Figaro
events.where: War Memorial Opera House, Civic Center
events.text: Mozart's comedy in Michael Cavanagh's production, conducted by Sebastian Weigle in his company debut, with Peter Kellner as Figaro and Slávka Zámečníková as Susanna. It runs 3 hours 45 minutes, and Sunday has limited availability.

events.name: Bhangra & Beats Diwali Night Market
events.where: Yerba Buena Gardens and Jessie Square, SoMa
events.text: A free, all-ages night market with bhangra music, DJs, dance lessons, Indian street food, mehndi, sari wrapping and an outdoor bazaar of local vendors. RSVP is encouraged.

events.name: Ferry Plaza Farmers Market
events.text: The Saturday market outside the Ferry Building, with California growers, bakers and food stalls, is the city's best place to see what is in season; go early, before the tea festival opens inside.

events.name: SF International Tea Festival
events.text: More than 30 tea makers and hundreds of teas to taste, with a porcelain tasting cup included in the ticket.

events.name: Renegade Craft Fair: Winter
events.where: Fort Mason Center Festival Pavilion, Marina
events.text: The winter edition of the big independent makers' fair, with ceramics, prints, jewelry and clothing: an early start on holiday shopping. Check hours on the fair's site.

events.name: Type for All! Ten Years of Type West (closing)
events.when: Sun. 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., closed 1:30 to 2 p.m.
events.text: The last day of the archive's show on a decade of its type-design program, with fonts from 31 countries. Admission is $10.

know: From SFO, BART runs straight to downtown (Powell Street or Embarcadero) in about half an hour; a taxi or rideshare takes 25 to 40 minutes depending on traffic. From Oakland, take the BART airport connector and change toward San Francisco.

A Clipper card, or Clipper in your phone's wallet, works on Muni buses, the T Third and other light-rail lines, and BART. The 38 Geary and 22 Fillmore buses cover most of Friday and Saturday; cable cars cost extra.
Tip 18 to 22 percent at sit-down restaurants. Many San Francisco menus add a separate surcharge for staff health care; it is not a tip, so read the bill.
Mid-November is the start of the rainy season and the days are short, with sunset around 5 p.m. Pack a rain shell and a warm layer, especially for the coast at Lands End.
Watch the day-of-week hours: the Exploratorium opens at noon on Sunday, the Japanese Tea Garden closes at 4:45 p.m. in November, and Letterform Archive is closed Monday to Wednesday.
The Warriors are on the road all weekend, so there are no Chase Center crowds on the T Third line. The opera runs past 11 p.m. on Friday, so plan a taxi or check late Muni service home.
